1.1: 1.1 The words of Nehemiah the son. Bede on Esdras, vol. 2: Nehemiah is interpreted consoler of the Lord, etc., up to: as they restore the walls of Jerusalem destroyed by enemies. The words of Nehemiah. The same, ibid.: Thus far the words of Esdras, etc., up to: who rejoice not to be weakened by temporal blandishments, but to be exercised by adversities and prepared for everlasting rest. In the month of Chislev. The same, ibid.: The month Chislev is the one we call December, the ninth among the Hebrews, the last with us. Its name, which is interpreted his hope, agrees well with the desires of him who was intent on raising up the ruins of the holy city. For the first foundation of good action is to have hope of the help of the Lord to accomplish what we desire. In this month the Lord was born, by whose name it was long before figured that in that month the true Nehemiah, long desired, would come for the building of the Church. I was in Susa. The same, ibid.: Susa is a metropolis of the Persians, but of such strength that it seems a fortress, and is interpreted riding or returning, which is fittingly applied to the faithful, especially to those who take care of the captivity of Jerusalem, that is, of the salvation of those who, having been at some time snatched from the Church by the snares of the devil, are brought back by the grace of God as penitents. For such are in the returning fortress, that is, in the strength of the mind recalled from the lowest things to desire of the heavenly fatherland, and in the cavalry of holy hearts, which carry God as their rider. Who remained. The same, ibid.: The sense of the letter is plain, etc., up to: they ought to have kept out the unworthy, to perish in the fire of avarice, lust and the other vices.
1.4: 1.4 I wept and mourned. If a holy man, hearing of the destruction of buildings of wood and stone, rightly mourned, fasted and prayed, sitting long in sadness, how much more in the destruction and ruin of souls ought we to persist in continual mourning and prayers, that by the mercy of God they may be raised to their former safety, who lay in the reproach of religion, with the enemy triumphing, squalid with the long filth of vices.
2.1: 2.1 And it came to pass. Bede on Esdras: Which is the first month of the year, etc., up to: to make known his own. He was indeed the king's cupbearer, he handed the cup to the king, he performed outwardly an office of gladness, but inwardly he mourned: because the holy city was torn down, etc. Hence: By the rivers of Babylon there we sat, etc. Psalm 126.
2.5: 2.5 If it seem good, etc. The same, ibid.: As by Cyrus, the first king of the Persians, Christ is signified, etc., up to: of which the whole sentence of the prophet I have taken care to set out as fully as I could in the book of times.
2.10: 2.10 And they heard. Heretics are grieved, etc., up to: and they know that those who erred by sinning return by repenting.
2.15: 2.15 I considered the wall of Jerusalem. He ranges about, surveying the various places of the destroyed city, and anxiously examines how each should be repaired. It is also the duty of spiritual teachers to rise often by night, and with careful search to inspect the state of the Church while the rest are at rest, that they may watchfully inquire how to correct and raise up what has been defiled or cast down by the wars of vices. The wall of Jerusalem lies scattered, and the conduct of the faithful is foul with earthly and weak affections. The gates are consumed by fire, when those who ought to open to others the entrance of life, having left the common master of truth, with the rest grow torpid in sloth, and serve temporal cares.
2.17: 2.17 Because Jerusalem is desolate. Bede, ibid.: These things are plain and fitting in the spiritual sense: because teachers, indeed all who burn with zeal for God, are in the greatest affliction, as long as they see Jerusalem, that is the vision of peace, which God has left and commended to us, laid desolate by the wars of dissensions: and the gates of virtues, which according to Isaiah praise ought to have occupied, cast down, the gates of hell prevailing, and held in reproach.
3.1: 3.1 And Eliashib the priest rose up. Bede on Esdras, vol. 2, book 3: That is, the high priest of that time, son of Joiakim, who after his father Jeshua the son of Jozadak held the priesthood for no short time. And rightly the restoration of the city began from the great priest and his brethren: so that those who had preceded in the degree of order might become an example to others in good works. And it is well joined to the priests as builders: And up to the tower of a hundred cubits they sanctified it, up to the tower of Hananel. For priests build in the hundredfold number of cubits, when they kindle all whom they teach with love and desire of eternal things. For a hundred, which in the reckoning of the fingers passes from the left hand to the right, figures heavenly goods, which in comparison with earthly things are as the right hand to the left. And they built. The same, ibid.: The old translation has, etc., up to: and in it let them be washed. The same, ibid.: It seems literally, etc., up to: they stretch out with the sole intention of the inner reward. The sheep gate. Which, namely, faces Joppa and Diospolis, that is Lydda, nearer the sea among all the ways of Jerusalem; which is now said to be called the gate of David, and to be the first of the gates to the west of Mount Sion. The Chronicles seem to agree with this opinion, where it is written of Manasseh king of Judah: After this he built a wall outside the city of David, etc. 2 Chron. 12. Bede, ibid.: Typically, however, as the flock signifies the faithful of the Lord, etc., up to: and in the times of Hezekiah the wall of the city was doubled, as the Chronicles show thus: He built also diligently all the wall, etc. 2 Chron. 23. Typically, moreover, this Zephaniah heard the voice of a cry from the fish gate and a howling from the second: because he foreknew that each would be cast down by enemies. For he saw that the faith and works of the teachers, by which the rest ought to be rescued from the waves of corruptible life and brought into the Church, were to be laid low on the earth by the snares of the devil, that is, that they would be deprived of heavenly joys through the appetite of earthly pleasure. And well from each gate, the first, namely, and the second, the inner and the outer, he heard the voice of cry and howling: because he saw that outwardly the works, and inwardly the hearts, were to be overthrown by the devil's assault. But because the Lord raises up the broken, Nehemiah relates that the fish gate was restored after its ruin: because if any of the preachers fall by sinning, there will not be wanting until the end of the age those who, succeeding, with the Lord's help will open to the faithful the gates of justice by living well and preaching. They themselves covered. The same, ibid.: This verse also concerning the other gates, etc., up to: who bring us more danger by praising than they bring back salutary help from us by seeing.
3.6: 3.6 At the old gate. Of which John says: Beloved, I write no new commandment to you, but an old commandment which you had from the beginning (1 John 2). The old commandment is the word which you have heard. The old gate is built in Jerusalem when the word of faith and love which was handed down from the beginning of the Church is either recovered among those who err, or established in the newly believing.
3.8: 3.8 At the wall. Namely the firmness and fortification of perfect love in the hearts of the elect, to which its instructors come by building, when, advancing in works of charity, they say: I have run the way of your commandments, etc. Ps. 118, by that enlargement, namely, of the enlightened mind, which loves both the friend in God and the enemy for the sake of God.
3.13: 3.13 And the valley gate. Bede, as above: The valley of Jehoshaphat, which is also Gehennon, etc., up to: that is, the humble by the gift of heavenly refreshment. And the valley gate. The same, ibid.: Well after the old gate and the wall of the broader street the valley gate is built, because after the rudiments of the Catholic faith, which works by love, it is necessary that humility be inculcated in us, to be held as it were the guardian of virtues, that the greater we are, the more we may be humbled in all things. And a thousand. The same, ibid.: They say that the site of the city of Jerusalem, etc., up to: that they may cast out from themselves all the rubbish of harmful action, useless speech, and even superfluous thought.
3.15: 3.15 And Shallum the son built the fountain gate, etc. The same, ibid.: Writers relate, etc., up to: comparing the steps with the growth of the Church itself and the advances of good works, which are done through humility. From the city of David, etc. The city of David, literally, is called Mount Sion, which, placed on the south, stands above the city as a citadel, and the greater part of the city lies below the mountain in the plain of a lower hill. Hence in the book of Kings: And David took the stronghold of Sion, this is the city of David (2 Kings 5). And a little after: And David dwelt in the stronghold, and called it the city of David, ibid.
3.16: 3.16 Nehemiah the son of Azbuk built, etc. Bede, as above: After the fountain gate and the walls of the pool of Siloam, etc., up to: and let them know that they will ascend to the heavenly kingdom. Over against the sepulchre of David, etc. The same, ibid.: Note that David was buried not in Bethlehem, as some think, but in Jerusalem, for a sure reason of mystery. For as, born in Bethlehem and anointed king, he figured Christ who was to be born in the same place from his seed, and to be adored by the magi in the person of a king; so dying and buried in Jerusalem, he figured Christ who was to suffer and be buried in the same city. To the pool, etc. The same, ibid.: The pool, namely divine Scripture, etc., up to: and if the ancient enemy takes from us the fountain of the word of God, he immediately bursts into the citadel of the mind.
3.19: 3.19 And he built, etc. The same, ibid.: Thus far the first wall of the city is built, etc., up to: in which we offend the eyes of inner judgment. Over against the ascent, etc. This is Christ, who in his faith and love united the people of the Jews and of the Gentiles: hence he is called the cornerstone. Over against whose ascent the second measure is built, when through purity of pious thought we tend to the vision of him, when even held in this life we sigh with frequent desire of his vision. There follow very many ranks of builders who are narrated to have built the second measure: because the greatest structure of the Church is in the fortification of inner virtue, when, namely, we guard our heart with all custody, since from it life proceeds. To draw each particular to spiritual understanding would be too long.
3.26: 3.26 The Nethinim. They are called Gibeonites, who in faithful devotion served in the ministry of the house of the Lord according to the arrangement of Joshua the son of Nun. In Ophel. Bede, ibid.: It was a tower not far from the temple, of enormous height. Hence it received the name Ophel, that is, of darkness or cloudiness, because it thrust its head into the clouds. Finally, where it is written in Micah: And you, cloudy tower of the flock (Mic. 4), the tower of Ophel is blessed. In which part of the city this tower is, the book of Chronicles shows, saying that Manasseh built a wall outside the city of David on the west of Gihon in the valley, from the entrance of the fish gate round about to Ophel (2 Chron. 33). It was fitting, therefore, according to the situation of the place, that the ministers of the temple should dwell in a tower near the temple. Mystically, however, the Nethinim dwell in Ophel, that is, in the cloudy tower, when those who by profession of a more perfect life are dedicated to God abide always in the fortification and height of virtues by action and thought, and their conversation is in heaven, of whom the crowd in admiration says: Who are these that fly as clouds? (Isa. 60), etc. Likewise the Tekoites dwell in Ophel, when certain men conspicuous by the habit of religion, with an enlightened heart, penetrate and constantly read and meditate on the hidden things of the Scriptures, of which it is written: Dark water in the clouds of the air (Ps. 17), that is, mystical knowledge in the prophets. Over against. Bede, ibid.: The Lord, namely, who daily waters us by the grace of his mercy, lest we slip and fail in the hardships of the present life, etc., up to: and because after the present gifts of virtues one ascends to see the glory of the Lord, it is rightly added: After him the Tekoites built, etc.
3.27: 3.27 From the tower. From the great and lofty tower the structure of the city reaches to the wall of the temple, when the just ascend from the height of contemplation, which in this life, temporal things despised, suspends the mind to heavenly desires, truly in that life to behold the glory of the Lord's incarnation, the glory of divine eternity also being laid open. And because Tekoa is interpreted trumpet or horn, and the Tekoites trumpeters, it is aptly said that the Tekoites built this. For it belongs to teachers, whose sound goes out into all the earth, to make known to the faithful, who are his city, the gifts of God, present or future. To the wall of the temple. The body of Christ, namely, of which it is said in John 2: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up: which the persecutors destroyed in death, but those who love him do not cease to see it raised up and exalted to the heavens in glory.
3.28: 3.28 But above, etc. Bede, ibid.: Jeremiah signifies that this gate is in the eastern quarter of the city, etc., up to: horses, when taken in a good sense, like asses, camels and mules, show the peoples of the Gentiles converted to the Lord, or the cares of temporal things subjected to the Lord of the soul. The priests built, etc. The priests of the city of God build the wall to the water gate when teachers, after the calling of the Jews, come, by sowing the word of God, to bring the Gentiles into the Church. Bede, ibid.: It is long to treat mystically of each building or builder, etc., up to: he writes the names in heaven.
4.1: 4.1 ... Sanballat ... greatly moved, mocked the Jews. Bede on Esdras, book 3, chap. 19, vol. 2: Plainly it is the wrath of heretics. These are the words of those who surname themselves Samaritans, that is, keepers of the law of God, etc., up to: and, amended in their ways, may obtain the ornaments of virtues.
4.3: 4.3 But Tobiah also, etc. The same, ibid.: The person and words of this Tobiah suit heretics, etc., up to: by which they strive to corrupt the fruitful minds of the faithful.
4.9: 4.9 And we prayed. This is the sole refuge against the enemies of the Church, namely prayer to God, and the diligence of teachers, who, meditating on his law day and night, fortify the hearts of the faithful against the snares of the devil and his soldiers by preaching, consoling and exhorting.
4.10: 4.10 The rubbish is too much. Bede, ibid.: Heaped up, namely, in the place of the wall, etc., up to: and for the house or the city, when the storm of temptation falls upon it, he who built is proved to have built to ruin.
4.11: 4.11 Our enemies said, etc. These things usually happen in the spiritual building; for the unwearied enemy remains with his satellites, namely unclean spirits and malicious men, who strive to hinder and overthrow the works of virtue and faith in us when we are unwary, and to slay the mind of the faithful with the sword of evil suggestion. But against these we must take up the armor of God, that we may be able to resist in the evil day, and stand perfect in all things.
4.13: 4.13 I set in the place, etc. That, surrounded by a band of armed men, the workers might build more freely and securely. For the ranks of the faithful are divided: some, adorning the Church within with good works, build; others, fortified with the arms of sacred reading, keep watch against the assaulting heretics. These strengthen their neighbors in the truth of faith with religious devotion, those wage the necessary conflict against the darts of the devil or of vices, and drive away from the Lord's fold the lurking wolves by pastoral solicitude.
4.16: 4.16 From that day, half, etc. Bede, ibid., chap. 20: It is to be noted that not only half of the young men did the work, etc., up to: and it is a lesser labor to avoid unknown carnal pleasure than to reject it once known.
4.22: 4.22 And let there be watches for you by night and day. The same, ibid.: Note how great zeal they had in working, etc., up to: they drive away from the Church by rebuking those who contradict.
5.1: 5.1 And there was a cry, etc. Bede on Esdras, book 3, chap. 21: The people desired to build the wall, etc., up to: and turning our hands from our own pleasures, let him convert them to building the city of Christ. The same, ibid.: The cry of the people is increased from three causes. Some, compelled by hunger, were willing to sell their sons to the richer: others, sparing their children, rather their fields and houses. Some, forbidding the sale of children and fields, only persuaded this, that they borrow money for the king's tribute, pledging fields and vineyards, until, fertility returning, they could repay the lenders what they had borrowed.
5.7: 5.7 And I rebuked the nobles, etc. Bede, ibid.: As the best leader of the heavenly army and wise architect of the city of God, etc., up to: that the Father may forgive us our debts.
5.13: 5.13 Also I shook my lap, and said: So may God shake out every man, etc. A terrible closing is put to this sentence. For whoever does not show mercy to the poor, or as though justly exacts from those who have not, is shaken out of his house, that is, from the assembly of the Church, in which he thought he would remain forever, and from his labors, namely, in the fruits of good works, in which he thought he had laboured laudably: he will receive nothing at all of labor. For labors without piety cannot be fruitful before God. And all the multitude said, Amen. How much the rebuke or imprecation of Nehemiah moved the hearts of all is shown: for, hearing the adjuration, answering, amen, and praising God, they did what he had commanded. In which it is plain that they received his words not from fear, but from love.
5.14: 5.14 For twelve years. Bede, as above: The Apostle expounds this, saying: The Lord ordained that they who preach the Gospel should live by the Gospel: but I have used none of these things (1 Cor. 9). For twelve years Nehemiah and his brethren so lived in the governorship that they did not eat the allowances which were due to governors: intimating that it is an evangelical work in the government of the people to exercise the work of ruler notably around the Church, and not to seek earthly advantage from subjects.
6.2: 6.2 Come, and let us make a covenant, etc. Bede on Esdras, book 3, chap. 23, vol. 2: The enemies of the holy city persuaded Nehemiah to come down into the plains, etc., up to: because the crafty enemy always tries to hinder our hands, let us take care always to strengthen them with divine help.
6.10: 6.10 And he entered. Nehemiah, beset by the snares of the enemies, enters the house of Shemaiah as a friend and brother, but finds him a plotter and enemy, as though corrupted by the gifts and friendship of foreigners. For the elect always have fights without, fears within, and not only the apostles but also the prophets led a life suspect with perils from their own kind, perils from the Gentiles, perils from false brethren.
6.15: 6.15 The month of Elul. Bede, as above: Which according to the Hebrews is the sixth, etc., up to: and henceforth let them adorn themselves with good works in the love of God and neighbor.
6.16: 6.16 All the nations. The same, ibid.: But those who wished to terrify the builders of the holy city, etc., up to: and driven out of the Church.
7.1: 7.1 Now after the wall was built, etc. Bede on Esdras, book 3, chap. 24, vol. 2: Mystically: when the wall of the Church has been built, new peoples being gathered to the faith or those who had erred being corrected, the doors of regular discipline must soon be set up; lest the devil, who goes about like a roaring lion, be able to break into the fold of God. I numbered the porters. The same, ibid.: The porters, who, namely, received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, that they may admit the worthy and humble; but keep the proud and unworthy from entrance to the heavenly city, saying: You have no part nor lot in this matter. For your heart is not right before God (Acts 8).
7.3: 7.3 Let not the gates be opened ... until the heat of the sun, etc. The same, ibid., that is, during the whole time of night, etc., up to: hence: And its gates shall not be shut by day, for there shall be no night there (Apoc. 21). And I set watchmen. The same, ibid.: Guardians of souls are not to be appointed from neophytes or from the common people, but from those who, freed by the grace of God from the conflict of vices, now have their mind in Jerusalem, that is in the vision of tranquil peace, whose conversation is in heaven. For when some, their course finished, are withdrawn from this light, others are soon put in their place, and never are lacking those who by keeping watch encompass the peace of the Church because of the fears of the night, according to that: Instead of your fathers sons are born to you (Ps. 44). These things typically fit that time when, the word of God having been sown far and wide by the apostles, the whole world received the new seed of faith, and the Church was not yet built, but the people were as yet rude, imbued only by hearing the word and by the sacraments. Therefore, having gathered not only the nobles but also the common people, he took care to number them diligently, that, the sum of all being seen, he could determine who ought to dwell in Jerusalem, who in other cities. Every one over against his own house. For thus the guarding of the holy Church is duly accomplished, if each so bears the solicitude of all the faithful that he bestows the care of more diligent zeal specially on those to whom, by God's authorship, he has been set over.
7.66: 7.66 All the multitude as one man. Josephus: He also commanded the people who tilled the fields to offer the tithes of the fruits at Jerusalem, so that the priests and Levites, having sustenance, might not abandon the perpetual rights of religion. And these gladly followed the decrees of Nehemiah. From then on the city came to be filled with a multitude of men. Nehemiah, having done many such good things worthy of praise, with the greatest magnificence, reached old age and died.
8.1: 8.1 And the seventh month was come. Bede on Esdras, book 3, chap. 26, vol. 2: Which was not far off. For when the wall was finished on the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month, only five days remained to the beginning of the seventh month, which from the first day to the twenty-second was wholly consecrated to the lawful ceremonies, which having been duly celebrated, he then returned with the princes and the people to arrange the dwellers of the city. And all the people were gathered together as one man to the street which, etc. Bede, ibid.: The devotion and concord of the people is to be noted, etc., up to: by whose song the people among prayers and sacrifices might be roused more ardently to the memory of the law. Mystically also, when the city is built, divine reading ought to follow, and the trumpets sound more frequently, that the people, initiated by the heavenly sacraments, may also by the sacred words be instructed more skillfully in season how they ought to live. Before the water gate. The same, ibid.: I think the water gate is said to be in the court of the priests, etc., up to: well therefore was the people gathered before the water gate, as if by its high priest to be spiritually given to drink of the streams of the Scriptures.
8.4: 8.4 And Ezra the scribe stood upon a step. The same, ibid.: He seems to remember, etc., up to: so that, timid and ashamed, he foretells to others by doing what he himself has not done, etc. When prelates excel their subjects as much in work as in honor, the subjects, roused by their examples, devoutly pursue the degree of their life, and, piously admonished by them, delight to pour out tears for sins or for desire of the heavenly fatherland. Hence it is well added, for all the people wept when they heard the words of the law, etc.
8.10: 8.10 Go, eat, etc. The same, ibid.: That we may strengthen the weaker consciences of our neighbors by the example of pious action and the sweetness of devout admonition, he commands that they be filled as with fat and richness, and that others may praise the name of the Lord with exultation. Literally also, when on feast days after prayer, reading and the diligence of psalms are completed we refresh the flesh, we ought to remember the poor and strangers. Be not sad. The teachers who rouse the minds of hearers to tears by sacred readings also console them, while they promise the joys that will follow.
8.11: 8.11 For it is a holy day. While, namely, we give attention to hearing and fulfilling the words of the Lord, on which day, though outwardly suffering adversities, we ought to rejoice in hope. Hence: As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing (2 Cor. 6), etc.
8.14: 8.14 And they found, etc. Bede, as above: These things are written more fully in Leviticus, etc., up to: we must remember that we are sojourners on the earth, and strangers as all our fathers were (Ps. 38).
8.15: 8.15 Of the most beautiful tree, etc. The same, ibid.: Which the Hebrews call the cedar. The boughs of myrtle bring a shade to him who can say, We are the good odor of Christ unto God in every place (2 Cor. 2). The boughs of the most beautiful tree and the boughs of myrtle, etc. The fruits of charity, which is the most beautiful among all the virtues, through which Christ also ascended the wood of the cross for our salvation, whose passion, while we imitate it as much as we can, we are protected by the boughs of the most beautiful tree and of myrtle for the mortification of vices and lusts. For the magi, offering myrrh to the Lord, taught that those who are Christ's crucify their flesh with its vices and concupiscences. The branches of palms. The same, ibid.: We bring branches of palms, which is the ornament of a victorious hand, when we bear a mind victorious over vices, and unconquered by all enemies, that we may stand before the throne in the sight of the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in our hands (Apoc. 7).
8.16: 8.16 Every one on his roof. The same, ibid.: On his roof, etc., up to: and may we deserve to abound in the greater fruits of good action.
8.18: 8.18 For seven days. The same, ibid.: The feast of tabernacles was kept for seven days, etc., up to: gathered in the sight of God, and never to be separated, has rejoiced.
9.1: 9.1 And on the day, etc. Bede, as above, chap. 28: The devotion of the corrected people is to be noted, etc., up to: when from other labors one rests, the ears are more freely lent to the divine readings. And Ezra said. Up to the end of his prayer or confession, what was said above, that they confessed their sins and the sins of their fathers, is shown more fully, Ezra praying, how it came about.
9.38: 9.38 Upon all these things therefore. Bede on Esdras, book 3, vol. 2: He shows with how great devotion all their persons held a new assembly after the feast of tabernacles, that, namely, with all intention they might unite themselves, purged from the contagion of crimes, to the divine covenant, and confirm the condition of the holy covenant by word and writing; and so, separated from the company of the impious, they might the more securely fulfill the work they had long begun, that is, that they might appoint fitting citizens of the city from the number of the impious.
10.1: 10.1 The sealers, etc. Another translation: Nehemiah, who is called Athersatha, for he had two names, whence in the singular is added the son of Hachaliah, which above is said more plainly: And Nehemiah said, and he is Athersatha (2 Esd. 7). The same, ibid.: For us also a spiritual sabbath is always to be kept, etc., up to: on the first day it is necessary to be cleansed from evils, then to be adorned with good acts.
11.1: 11.1 And they dwelt. Bede on Esdras, book 3, vol. 2: Now the arrangement is complete, etc., up to: but they receive by the gift of the hidden judge and bestower.
11.3: 11.3 And in Jerusalem. The same, ibid.: By these words it is shown, etc., up to: for it follows: Of the children of Judah dwelt in Kiriath-arba (2 Esd. 11). The same, ibid.: Judah is interpreted confessing or confession, etc., up to: when one of those who are in the field shall be taken, and the other left.
12.1: 12.1 Now these are, etc. Bede, as above: Here the chief priests together with their brethren, etc., up to: and therefore he could have been born while Nehemiah was still alive. Bede, ibid.: The succession of the chief priests and Levites is described, etc., up to: they restore with friendly provision, and exalt with due honor. The same, ibid.: The city had long been built, etc., up to: then in the very thing itself, of the blessed men enjoying the divine vision in spiritual bodies among the angelic hosts.
12.27: 12.27 And with cymbals, etc. The same, ibid.: Cymbals, psalteries and harps, etc., up to: and they kindle the hearts of their neighbors to love of him, etc.
12.28: 12.28 The sons of the singers. The same, ibid.: The imitators of them, namely, etc., up to: and at the very time of the dedication, that is, of the perpetual recompense, are likewise united there.
12.30: 12.30 And they were purified. The same, ibid.: The order is altogether just, etc., up to: and with hands and feet bound be cast into outer darkness.
12.31: 12.31 The princes of Judah, etc., that is of confession or praise, are the more perfect teachers of the Church, who at the dedication of the city go up upon the wall: because in the time of tribulation they are proved to have surpassed the general conduct of the Church by living on a higher plane. For of these it is said: Upon your walls, O Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen (Isa. 62), etc. Rightly therefore those who now preside over the walls of the Church as watchmen will then also be preeminent in the glory of recompense. And I appointed two choirs. Or they purge the filth of sinners from the Church in the present by living more correctly and correcting the erring, and in the future expel from the city of the Lord, that is from entrance to the heavenly fatherland, those who would not be corrected, by judicial power. Or the choirs of those praising, going to the right upon the wall, go up to the dung gate, while they proclaim worthy of praise those who remove all uncleanness from the Church by preaching, rebuking, excommunicating.
12.34: 12.34 And of the sons of the priests, etc. In this life the sons of the priests sound with trumpets at the dedication of the city of God, who by preaching kindle the hearts of the hearers to the memory of the heavenly fatherland.
12.35: 12.35 With the instruments of the song of David. Because they rely not on their own sense or desires, but, following in all things the life and doctrine of the fathers and prophets, they persist in the word of preaching. And Ezra the scribe. Because in all that they do they have before their eyes the words of holy Scripture, under whose guidance they come to the entrance of eternal life, that they may be inebriated with the plenty of the house of God, and with the torrent of his pleasure, with whom is the fountain of life, etc.
12.36: 12.36 And over against them they went up by the steps. Bede, ibid.: When the city was being built, etc., up to: they celebrate the holy Trinity with joint exultation. Above the house of David. The same, ibid.: The sons of the priests go up, etc., up to: and are worthy to see the rising of the sun of justice without setting.
12.37: 12.37 And above the tower of the furnaces. The same, ibid.: It is long to discourse specially on each gate or tower, etc., up to: it is necessary to be fortified always with circumspect caution and solicitude.
12.39: 12.39 And the two choirs stood. The same, ibid.: The walls and gates of the city having been walked around, etc., up to: in fulfilling whose will I remain with unwearied mind.
12.41: 12.41 And they sang clearly. You have broken my bonds: to you I will sacrifice the sacrifice of praise. I will pay my vows to the Lord in the courts of the house of the Lord, in the sight of all his people, in the midst of you, O Jerusalem (Ps. 115). This is done when in the heavenly fatherland, the multitude of all the saints being gathered, we offer those praises for which we now groan, and which we thirst for with daily desire in thanksgiving.
12.42: 12.42 For God had made them rejoice, etc. Bede, ibid.: These things at the dedication of the holy city, etc., up to: and they took care to offer the greatest victims of good works. And the wives also, etc. Because at the time of the resurrection not only those who by preaching or by working strongly built the Church receive the fruit of labor, but even the weaker companions of the same faith rejoice in the same receiving of life. For the Lord has blessed the little ones with the greater (Ps. 113).
12.43: 12.43 And they numbered also, etc. Bede, ibid.: All rejoicing, etc., up to: and it was dedicated with great praise and gladness.
13.1: 13.1 And on that day it was read, etc. Bede on Esdras, book 3, vol. 2: These, because they were born of incest, etc., up to: but God turned the curse of Balaam into a blessing for his people, and fortified him from the arms of enemies.
13.3: 13.3 Now it came to pass, etc. Because we must attend to the hearing of truth, where when we are forbidden by divine reading any one vice, immediately also whatever of defiling vice we find in ourselves we cast away from our action and conscience.
13.6: 13.6 In all these things. Bede, ibid.: This sentence, etc., up to: which Nehemiah, returning, soon rooted out.
13.8: 13.8 And I cast forth the vessels of the house of Tobiah. The same, ibid.: He who is mentioned above, a servant, an Ammonite, enemy of the people of God, etc., up to: what communion heretics and schismatics have with the orthodox and peaceful sons of God. And I cast forth. The same, ibid.: You also, whatever of unfaithfulness and uncleanness you find among the faithful, etc., up to: for as Nehemiah in the rest, so in this also he represented his person. The same, ibid.: For six days we are bidden by the law to work the necessary things, on the seventh to rest, etc., up to: let them by all means turn their gaze from those things which pertain to food and clothing, but dispense them with fitting moderation.
13.16: 13.16 Bringing fish and all things, etc. The same, ibid.: The good fish is pious faith, which the wicked from the Lord, a weak thought that plunges itself beyond measure into the cares of this world, which the Tyrians, that is the narrowed, seek to sell us on the sabbath, when unclean spirits try to overwhelm the rest of our thought with the deep cares of the world untimely. But for such a trade Nehemiah rebukes and chastises the nobles of Judah, while divine inspiration purges those who strive to serve the profession of piety from such thoughts.
13.19: 13.19 And it came to pass. Bede, ibid.: Our conscience, etc., up to: therefore what follows deservedly follows.
13.22: 13.22 I said also to the Levites that they should be purified, etc. The same, ibid.: It is necessary that they be cleansed from daily exercise of work, etc., up to: it is fitting that they first purify their mind and acts from all stain of errors.
13.23: 13.23 But also in those days. The same, ibid.: In the Church they take foreign wives, etc., up to: but interpreting with a Gentile sense.
13.30: 13.30 Therefore I cleansed them. The same, ibid.: More plainly in all things the end is worthy of the building of the holy city and the temple of the Lord, that, the citizens being cleansed of pollution foreign to God, the orders of priests and Levites may be duly kept in their ministry, that the teachers of the Church, regularly appointed, may exhort the people, chastened from every sin, henceforth to remain and always grow in good.
13.31: 13.31 And for the offering of wood at the times appointed, and for the firstfruits. Among other things the people offer wood to feed the fire of the altar, when they work works of virtue worthy of divine consecration. The wood burns and is consumed on the altar of holocausts, when in the hearts of the elect the works of justice are perfected by the flame of charity. Remember me, O my God, for good. Deservedly such a founder and dedicator of the city, after many labors of devotion, commends himself to the memory of the Creator and giver of all good things.
